title: Edge cache TTL desynchronization — customer notice and verification steps
body:
SUMMARY

What happened (short): On 2029-03-11 at ~09:07 UTC a subset of inference requests in two EU edge regions observed stale cached model prefix state that resulted in truncated or unexpectedly repeated structured outputs for affected tenants. We observed the first customer reports at 09:12 UTC and initiated a mitigation sequence that restored expected responses by 09:45 UTC for most traffic.

Customer-visible impact: Some API calls returned responses that had partially stale token prefixes (e.g., repeated closing tokens, truncated structured JSON arrays). This primarily impacted streaming and structured-output endpoints in the eu-west-1 and eu-west-3 edge clusters for roughly 30–40 minutes for a small percentage of requests. No customer data was exposed beyond normal request/response content.

STATUS PAGE UPDATE (for public status):
- Incident start: 2029-03-11 09:07 UTC
- Regions affected: eu-west-1, eu-west-3 (edge clusters)
- Symptom: intermittent stale prefix in cached inference responses causing truncation/repeat in structured outputs
- Current status: Service restored for the majority of traffic; mitigation complete as of 2029-03-11 09:45 UTC. Ongoing verification and follow-up remediation in progress.

DETAILED CUSTOMER-FACING EXPLAINER (for account contacts):
Root cause (plain language): An internal cache TTL/refresh coordination bug allowed a small set of edge cache nodes to serve cached prefix state that was not fully invalidated after a model routing change pushed the new prefix metadata. That stale prefix information could cause the streaming runtime to emit duplicate or truncated chunks in structured outputs when the request matched certain prefix/cache key patterns.

Why you saw the symptom: When a model routing update (background rollout) changed the prefix metadata used by the streaming runtime, most edge nodes invalidated or refreshed the cache correctly. A narrow race condition in the invalidation sequence for a small subset of nodes meant they served an out-of-date prefix for a short period. Requests that hit those nodes received outputs constructed with that stale state, which manifested as truncated arrays or repeated tokens in structured streams.

What we did (mitigation):
- 09:13 UTC: Detection and confirmed scope; moved traffic away from affected nodes using smart-routing policy to healthy variants.
- 09:18 UTC: Applied a targeted cache flush and forced prefix re-sync for the two affected edge clusters.
- 09:25 UTC: Deployed a temporary guarding patch to the edge invalidation sequence to prevent the race from reoccurring during the verification window.
- 09:45 UTC: Verified normal response distributions and resumed normal routing; began broader audit to ensure no residual stale caches.

Verification and results: Post-mitigation sampling and participant telemetry show that the occurrence rate dropped to near zero after the forced re-sync and routing shift. We reprocessed sampling logs for the 09:07–09:45 window and verified that affected requests were limited to a small fraction of overall throughput (<0.2% of requests in the two regions).

Customer impact details (what this means for your data and product):
- Data integrity: There is no evidence of data leakage to other tenants. The issue was limited to response construction on affected nodes and did not change request payloads or persisted customer artifacts.
- Retries: If your application observed a truncated structured response during the incident window, a safe non-destructive retry of the same API call (idempotent where possible) is the recommended path. Where calls are not idempotent, please contact us and we will provide per-tenant guidance.

Recommended immediate customer actions (concise list):
1) If you saw truncated or duplicated tokens in responses, retry the request. For streaming endpoints prefer re-opening the stream to let the runtime produce a fresh response instead of concatenating partial chunks.
2) For structured outputs (JSON arrays, tabular responses), perform the quick integrity checks below (Verification Checklist) before accepting results into downstream pipelines.
3) If you rely on strict ordering or exact-token semantics for production flows, temporarily enable your application-level validation gate (schema validator / checksum) and reject responses that fail, then trigger a controlled retry policy.

Verification Checklist (customer steps to self-validate):
- Confirm request timestamp: did the problematic response arrive between 09:07–09:45 UTC on 2029-03-11? If not, likely unaffected.
- Inspect for repeated closing tokens or duplicated array elements at the end of the payload.
- For streaming consumers: check for repeated chunk boundary markers that differ from your expected schema.
- If you have recorded evidence (request id, returned partial payload, timestamp), attach them to a ticket and we will prioritize inspection.

FAQ (short):
Q: Could this happen again?
A: The immediate race condition was mitigated with a guarding patch; a targeted fix for the invalidation coordination is scheduled for the next release (see "Planned next steps" below). We are also expanding targeted synthetic tests to exercise coordinated TTL invalidation across edge rollouts.

Q: Do you need us to resend requests or logs?
A: If you saw bad responses and the requests are idempotent, a retry is sufficient. If you have non-idempotent flows or recorded evidence, please upload the request id(s) and a copy of the response to the support ticket and include the approximate timestamp.

Q: Was customer data exposed?
A: No. This was a response construction artifact; there is no indication that any tenant could read another tenant's data.

Next steps (what Redwood is doing):
- Short term (in progress): Full audit of cache invalidation traces for affected clusters; follow-up warm restarts for edge nodes that logged the outdated prefix.
- Medium term (next 7 days): Ship a deterministic invalidation sequencer and add a cross-node TTL-sync handshake to the edge control plane to eliminate the observed race.
- Long term: Add cross-region synthetic traffic and end-to-end streaming verification to catch this class of regression earlier. We will publish a technical postmortem for engineering audiences once the medium-term fix is deployed.

Contact and escalation:
- For urgent needs or large-scale impact, open a priority ticket referencing INF-9876 and include "edge-cache-ttl-drift" in the subject; your CSM will be notified.
- Support channel: support@redwood.ai (include request id and timestamps where possible).

Draft status and ownership:
- Document owner: Maya Chen (customer-success)
- Reviewers: Liam O'Connor (ops), Priya Nair (SRE), Ezra Kim (platform eng)
- Status: in_review — intended to be used as both a concise status page update and a customer-facing post-incident verification note.

Notes to internal reviewers (short):
- Consider adding a short sanitized example (before/after response) for customers who are developers and will want to see the exact symptom pattern.
- Confirm whether we want to offer passive opt-in reprocessing for customers with non-idempotent flows — this will require legal/ops signoff.
